text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

The white sugar market in London remained unimpressed by forecasts of a significant sugar surplus in Pakistan in 1997/98 as well as by the extremely favourable beet test results from France. October closed $2.80 higher at $322.90 per tonne. December added $2.40 to close at $320.90 per tonne.

Raw sugar futures in New York ended firmer across the board. Spot October added 15 points to close at 11.53 cents/lb, while March closed 16 points higher at 11.81 cents/lb. The market remains optimistic concerning the future development of prices as fundamentals are expected to improve in 1997/98.

NETHERLANDS ** - The Sugar Research Institute (IRS) in its latest forecast pegged the likely beet yield per ha in 1997 at 60.1 tonnes, up from 56.0 tonnes in 1996 and above the 1987/96 average of 58.7 tonnes. Sugar yield in 1997 is forecast to reach 9.6 tonnes, white value, up from last year's figure of 9.3 tonnes and the average of also 9.3 tonnes. This means that sugar production in 1997/98 will remain above 1 million tonnes, white value, which compares to 1.035 million tonnes produced in 1996/97.

DENMARK - In spite of recent hot and dry weather prospects for a good harvest are not threatened, the Danish Department of Plant Production told Reuters. The department said the hot dry weather in recent weeks means that sugar beets lack water and have shrivelled to preserve what moisture they can. It was added that this did not necessarily threaten the harvest, due in early October, as precipitation would in all likelihood revive the beet by that time.

IRELAND - Crop prospects in Ireland, as in many other European countries, seem to be very good indeed. In its first beet test of August 8 the Irish Sugar Plc pegged root yield per ha at 40.67 tonnes, up from 30.92 tonnes last year and the 1992/96 average of 28.24 tonnes. However, sugar content was with 10.68 per cent lower than last year (12.24 per cent) and also below the average of 11.61 per cent. The sugar yield per ha on August 8 was 4.36 tonnes, white value, up from 3.73 tonnes last year and the average of 3.26 tonnes. Given the unchanged area sown to sugar beet the first test signals that production will be higher than last year's 227,000 tonnes, white value.

JAPAN ** - Japan imported 152,985 tonnes of sugar, raw value, in June 1997, 8 per cent less than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1996/97 (October) up to 1.253 million tonnes, slightly less than the 1.271 million tonnes imported the same period in 1995/96. Total imports in crop year 1995/96 (October/September) dropped to 1.681 million tonnes from 1.716 million tonnes the previous year. Main suppliers of raw sugar in October/June 1996/97 were Cuba (202,844 vs 81,361 tonnes), Thailand (375,424 vs 583,235 tonnes) and Australia (497,919 vs 469,433 tonnes).

AUSTRALIA ** - Australia exported 154,846 tonnes of sugar, raw value, in June 1997, the first month of the 1997/98 crop year, 11 per cent less than was exported the same month the previous year. Total exports in crop year 1996/97 (June/May) reached 4.344 million tonnes, up from 4.177 million tonnes exported the previous year. Main countries of destination for Australian raw sugar in June 1997 were Canada (61,800 tonnes), Indonesia (20,324 tonnes), South Korea (21,500 tonnes) and Malaysia (31,500 tonnes).

POLAND ** - Poland exported 29,397 tonnes of sugar, raw value, in May 1997, significantly up on the 201 tonnes exported the same month the previous year. That brought total exports since the beginning of 1996/97 (September) up to 262,586 tonnes which compares to 2,558 tonnes exported the same period in 1995/96. Total exports in crop year 1995/96 reached 4,440 tonnes, down from 14,828 tonnes exported the previous year. Main countries of destination for Polish white sugar in September/May 1996/97 were Russia (14,635 vs 382 tonnes), Uzbekistan (17,233 vs 0 tonnes), Algeria (23,279 vs 0 tonnes), Jordan (12,835 vs 0 tonnes) and Yemen (21,916 vs 0 tonnes).
